items.title: Patrick Stewart dies
items.text: Tributes have poured in from around the world following the death of renowned British actor Sir Patrick Stewart at the age of 86. His close friend and co-star Sir Ian McKellen praised him as one of the most respected actors of his generation. Stewart built a legendary career that seamlessly bridged classical Shakespearean theater and massive Hollywood blockbusters. Although he earned international fame playing Captain Jean-Luc Picard in Star Trek and Professor Charles Xavier in X-Men , he always remained deeply connected to his stage roots at the Royal Shakespeare Company. Directors and fellow actors remembered him as a generous collaborator who brought immense humanity, discipline, and accessibility to every role he played, and his passing marks a huge loss for stage and screen. His final film performance will serve as a lasting farewell to fans worldwide. Difficult words: seamlessly (smoothly and continuously), collaborator (a person who works jointly with others on a project or activity), farewell (saying goodbye). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

items.title: Patrick Stewart dies
items.text: Famous British actor Sir Patrick Stewart passed away at the age of 86. Many friends and fans are sharing kind words about his life and work. Actor Ian McKellen called him a deeply loved and respected friend. Stewart became famous around the world for his main roles in Star Trek and the X-Men movies, but he also loved playing in classical theater and performed in many famous Shakespeare plays in Britain. People who worked with him say he was a very talented, kind, and hardworking actor who made deep stories easy for everyone to enjoy. Fans will always remember his great voice, his classic movies, and his famous theater roles. Difficult words: classical theater (traditional plays and dramatic art), perform (to act, sing, dance, or play music in front of people). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

items.title: Patrick Stewart dies
items.text: Famous actor Sir Patrick Stewart dies at age 86. Many people around the world are sad today. Stewart is famous for his big roles in Star Trek and X-Men movies. He also loves acting on stage in big theater shows. His close friends say that he is a kind man. He loves his work very much. People love listening to his deep voice and watching him act. He shows that you can do big action movies and also play in old story plays on stage. Fans will miss him, but they can still watch his great films. Difficult words: sad (unhappy), stage (an area in a theater where actors are), miss (to feel sad because someone or something is no longer somewhere). items.title: A bull in a car
items.text: In Norfolk, the United States, police were surprised when they received reports of a man driving with a cow in his car, only to discover a massive Watusi bull as the passenger. This breed of African cattle is known for its gigantic horns. The driver, Lee Meyer, was stopped by the police, who issued him a warning due to the unusual and potentially unsafe situation. The bull named Howdy Doody could only fit in the car after modifications were made, including removing parts of the car’s body and windshield and installing a platform. The incident drew attention from onlookers, and it’s unclear where the bull and the driver were heading. Difficult words: breed (a particular type of animal or plant), modification (change), windshield (a window at the front of a car). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

items.title: A bull in a car
items.text: In Norfolk, the United States, the police responded to reports of a man driving with a cow in his car. When they stopped the car, they were surprised to find a massive Watusi bull as the passenger. The bull’s name was Howdy Doody, and the driver had to make some changes in his car to fit the bull in. This incident attracted attention from onlookers who called the police. It’s unclear where the bull and the driver were going. Difficult words: massive (very big), attention (when people are interested in something), onlooker (a person who sees something happen). items.title: A bull in a car
items.text: Something crazy happens in Norfolk, the United States. People see a big bull in the back of a car. The driver’s name is Lee Meyer. He makes some changes to his car. The bull fits in the car thanks to the changes. People, who see the car, call the police. The police stop the car. The bull is a big Watsui bull. This bull has really big horns . The police explain the driver that the situation is dangerous. An accident may happen. The bull’s name is Howdy Doody. Reports do not say where the man and the bull are going. Difficult words: fit (to be small enough to stay in a place), horn (a hard part on an animal’s head), explain (to make something clear). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

items.title: Man completes 28-year walk around the world
items.text: A British man has completed an amazing 28-year walk around the world. Former soldier Karl Bushby, 57, arrived home in the city of Hull in England on Monday. He started his adventure in November 1998 in Chile, South America. His plan was to walk all the way home without using cars, boats, buses, trains, or airplanes. During his journey, he travelled about 58,000 kilometres through 29 countries. He crossed frozen seas, deserts, mountains, and jungles. He also faced many dangers. These included encountering polar bears and kidnappers, and spending time in a Russian prison. His journey was expected to take 12 years. However, problems with money, visas, and borders made his trip a lot longer. Thousands of people welcomed Mr Bushby home. He was very happy to finally finish his journey. His mother was waiting outside his childhood home to greet him. Bushby joked: "Sorry to keep you waiting." He also told the cheering crowd that many people around the world had helped him get home. He said he could not have done it alone. Britain's Prime Minister congratulated him on his achievement. He praised Bushby's determination and belief in himself. Bushby told the Guardian newspaper that he wasn't so interested in walking. He said: "It's boring as hell." That didn't stop him walking across four continents. items.title: Study finds majority of pilots nod off mid-flight
items.text: A new report has raised serious concerns about pilot fatigue. The European Cockpit Association (ECA) conducted a survey of nearly 7,200 pilots across 32 countries. It discovered that exhaustion in the cockpit is a widespread and underreported problem. More than three-quarters of respondents said they had briefly dozed off while operating an aircraft in the month before the survey. Almost a quarter of them admitted they continued flying even when they were too tired. Furthermore, half said they had operated a flight when they should have declared themselves unfit for duty. Tiredness can result from long working hours, insufficient rest, and unpredictable schedules. The pilots were very frank in their answers to the survey questions. Many said they were reluctant to report fatigue because they feared punishment or other negative reactions from their bosses. Captain Coen George, a director of the ECA, warned: "When pilots fear career consequences, fatigue goes unreported and the risk returns to the cockpit." Aviation safety experts say exhaustion can impair judgement, slow reaction times and prevent pilots from responding effectively to unexpected in-flight situations. The experts urged airlines to foster a culture in which pilots can report tiredness without fear of repercussions. Carriers should ensure that passenger safety is their top priority. items.title: World-famous London shopping street pedestrianized
items.text: One of London's most famous shopping streets has been pedestrianized. This means no cars, buses, trucks, or motorbikes can enter it. The street is called Oxford Street. It is well known all over the world. It used to be full of traffic. The Mayor of London, Sir Sadiq Khan, decided to make it pedestrian-only. Around one kilometre of the street is off limits to vehicles. However, delivery trucks can use the area between midnight and 7 am. Mayor Khan hopes the pedestrianization will bring more shoppers back to the area. He called it a very important event for London. Mr Khan also plans to plant more trees along the street, create public squares, and add more seats and tables. There have been mixed reactions to the pedestrianization of Oxford Street. Many people support the plan. They are happy that the area will be less polluted. Khan said a traffic-free Oxford Street would "unlock the full potential" of an important area of London and help make a better, greener, and richer London. Around half a million people visit the street every day. However, many Londoners are unhappy that the street has been closed to traffic. Local official Tim Barnes said: "Traffic will be pushed to the small streets nearby causing economic and environmental harm." The Spectator magazine warned that life for car drivers would be harder. items.title: Mummy removed from exhibition over 'lack of consent'
items.text: A museum in Scotland has removed the remains of an ancient Egyptian mummy from an exhibition because there is no documented evidence that the deceased gave consent for their remains to be displayed. Glasgow's Kelvingrove Art Gallery and Museum took away the remains of a priest named Nakht, a mummified male head, and other body parts. In place of the exhibits, visitors found signs explaining that the remains had been removed "as a mark of respect". The museum said the decision "reflects contemporary museum practice". It added: "In the absence of consent, we believe removing ancient Egyptian human remains from display is more respectful to the deceased individuals." The decision has provoked widespread criticism. Scottish politician Murdo Fraser called the move "woke madness". He argued that museums should showcase history rather than hide it. A museum visitor complained that his daughter was upset at not being able to see the exhibits. An education campaigner said the decision "represents the triumph of educational stupidity and ignorance". He added: "It is not possible to seek permission from those who died thousands of years ago." However, the museum defended its action. It cited the International Council of Museums' Code of Ethics, which says museums "should uphold the inherent dignity of human remains". Buy my 1,000 Ideas and Activities for Language Teachers eBook. items.title: New EU deforestation law
items.text: The EU’s anti-deforestation law faces an enforcement test ahead of its launch on 30 December 2026. Under the new rules, companies selling goods such as palm oil, coffee, and cocoa must prove their products are not linked to land cleared after 2020. However, recent investigations by Indonesian environmental organizations reveal that major international consumer brands risk breaching these regulations. Reports show that companies like PepsiCo, Unilever, and Ferrero have bought palm oil from Indonesian plantations accused of recent illegal deforestation. Despite heavy political pressure and lobbying from major exporting nations like the United States and Indonesia to delay or soften the legislation, environmental activists insist the EU must strictly enforce the rules. Indonesia has lost vast areas of forest to illegal logging and agricultural clearing, which increased its vulnerability to severe wildfires. Experts emphasize that strict enforcement by European authorities will be essential to hold global corporations accountable and halt worldwide forest destruction. Difficult words: enforcement (compelling compliance with a law), lobby (to influence a politician or public official on an issue), vulnerability (the possibility of being attacked, damaged, or harmed). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

items.title: New EU deforestation law
items.text: The EU will start using new anti-deforestation rules on 30 December 2026. Companies which sell products like palm oil, coffee, and chocolate must prove they don’t cut down trees to make them. But environmental groups in Indonesia found that big international brands may be breaking these rules. Well-known companies like PepsiCo and Unilever recently bought palm oil from plantations linked to illegal forest clearing. Some countries, including the US and Indonesia, asked the EU to make the rules easier for businesses. But environmental activists say Europe must stay strong and enforce the law. Indonesia lost many forests to farming and fires, so strict checks are needed to protect nature and stop global forest destruction. Difficult words: anti-deforestation (about preventing or stopping the clearing of forests), brand (a product made by a company under a particular name), enforce (to make sure that a rule is followed). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

items.title: New EU deforestation law
items.text: The EU has a new rule to save forests. The rule is starting on 30 December 2026. Companies which sell things like coffee, palm oil, and chocolate must prove that they do not cut down trees. But some big companies are still buying palm oil from places in Indonesia. People cut down forests illegally there. Some countries want Europe to stop or change the rule. These countries are, for example, the US and Indonesia. But the EU must follow the rules strictly . Indonesia is losing many trees to big fires and farming. People hope that this new rule will stop companies from harming trees and help keep the earth green and safe. Difficult words: prove (to show that something is true), illegally (against rules), strictly (exactly). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

items.title: Chinese baby companies have problems
items.text: Chinese companies that produce children’s products are diversifying their offerings to include adult and pet clothing, as the country faces a record-low birth rate that is expected to continue declining. The demographic decline can be traced back to China’s one-child policy, which lasted from 1980 to 2015. While the limit has been raised to three children in 2021, couples are still reluctant to have babies. Yan Zhang, founder and CEO of Shanghai children’s clothing brand NATUNAKIDS, said the company’s sales have not been significantly impacted by the low birth rate yet but he expects sales to decrease over the next three to five years. The shift in the industry has left some consumers worried about their favorite brands going bankrupt. Market analyst Shaun Rein warns that companies in the baby industry will face declining margins , bad revenues , and falling stock prices. Difficult words: reluctant (unwilling to do something), margin (profit), revenue (income). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

items.title: Chinese baby companies have problems
items.text: Chinese companies that make products for children are expanding their product lines to include adult and pet clothing. The country’s falling birth rate is a result of the one-child policy that lasted from 1980 to 2015. The government raised the limit to three children in 2021, but couples are still not having babies. Yan Zhang, CEO of Shanghai children’s clothing brand NATUNAKIDS, expects sales to go down in the next three to five years. Customers worry that their favorite brands may go bankrupt as a result of the changes in the industry. Experts predict a bad future for baby companies in China. Difficult words: birth rate (how many children are born in a country in one year), brand (the name of products by one company), bankrupt (when a person or company has no money at all). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

items.title: Chinese baby companies have problems
items.text: In China, fewer children are born every year. This starts in 1980 when the government says that people can only have one child. Now, companies which make things for kids are having problems. In 2021, the government says that families can have three children. But people do not want them. Companies start clothes for adults and pets instead of products for babies. Experts believe that sales of these companies will go down in the next few years. People who like certain brands worry that the companies will end. Experts say that baby companies will have a hard time in the future. Difficult words: pet (an animal which people keep at home, for example, a cat or dog), sale (how much a company sells), brand (the name for products of one company). items.title: Man sells everything for AI dream "partner"
items.text: A man in Brazil had a sad experience in his search for love. Mr X, 49, sold everything he owned to get enough money to see a woman he met online. He travelled over 2,000 kilometres by bus. He first met her online in 2020 and fell in love with her. He wanted to marry her. Her name was Jessica. Her online profile read: "I really want to support you. I want you to come to my farm and never work again in your life." Mr X went to meet her in the city of Belo Horizonte, but he could not find her. He showed people photos of her, but nobody knew who she was. He then found out that she was not real. She was created by AI. The man was sad. He said: "I came here to find happiness." Mr X's story shows how risky it can be to look for love online. Many people feel lonely and want to find a partner. However, they can be easily tricked because AI can make people who look and sound real. Jessica's social media account had over 300,000 followers. She looked like a real woman. The person who created Jessica said they made her to get people's attention online. They wanted to use the AI Jessica to help sell things. Mr X wants people to be careful so they don't make a similar mistake in the future. It is important to check the identity of a person you meet online carefully. items.title: Influencers in Mexico work for drug groups
items.text: Ever since the Sinaloa Cartel split into rival groups in 2024, social media has turned into a dangerous battleground for Mexico’s drug wars. The competing factions regularly target popular content creators, and use them to show off power, post propaganda , and recruit young people. Local influencers who adopt narco culture for clicks often get caught in the middle and put themselves directly in the sights of rival gangs. On top of that, federal agents are looking into dozens of creators accused of helping cartels clean dirty money through online shops, brand deals, and live donations. This deadly connection has already cost the lives of at least 19 influencers across the country. Weak police work, a lack of real punishment, and slow moderation by tech platforms mean cartels can keep using young creators as easy tools for cash and influence online. Difficult words: faction (a small, organized group within a larger organization or political party), propaganda (information, ideas, or rumors deliberately spread to influence public opinion or promote a political cause), lack (not enough of something).
